hook: The queen who made herself pharaoh, and the stepson who tried to erase her from history.

pages.x: Hatshepsut was the daughter of the pharaoh Thutmose I and married her half-brother, Thutmose II. When he died, she ruled for her little stepson, Thutmose III. Within about seven years she had herself crowned pharaoh, with all the titles and power of a king.
pages.cap: Thutmose III, her stepson and co-ruler

pages.x: Egyptians expected a pharaoh to be a man, so many of her statues show Hatshepsut with a king's kilt, a broad chest and the false ceremonial beard pharaohs wore. Some inscriptions call her "His Majesty". Others show her plainly as a woman. She was making up the role as she went.

She sent a fleet down the Red Sea to the land of Punt, probably on the coast of Eritrea or Somalia. The ships came home loaded with gold, ebony, ivory, leopard skins, baboons and living myrrh trees, which were planted at her temple. Carvings of the trip, even of Punt's queen, still survive.

Across the Nile from Thebes, her architect Senenmut built her funeral temple: three broad terraces of columns rising against a wall of golden cliffs. Its name means "Holiest of Holies". It is one of the most beautiful buildings of the ancient world.

Late in his reign Thutmose III had her statues smashed and her name chiselled off monuments, perhaps so that no one would remember a woman as pharaoh. Her name vanished from the lists of kings. Archaeologists slowly pieced her story back together, and in 2007 her mummy was identified by a single tooth.

Hatshepsut ruled Egypt for about twenty years of peace and plenty and built some of its finest monuments. Someone tried to erase her, but she is now remembered as one of the most successful pharaohs, and one of the first great women rulers known to history.
pts: Ruled Egypt as pharaoh for about 20 years
Sent the famous trading voyage to Punt
Built the temple at Deir el-Bahari
